strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored question—scalability of GANs—by combining VAE-latent training with plain transformer backbones, an angle that has been thoroughly exploited for diffusion/AR models but not GANs.

Clear diagnosis of two concrete failure modes at scale (early-layer underutilization and scale-dependent optimization instability), each supported by targeted visual/quantitative evidence (PCA feature visualization, per-block LPIPS ablation in Fig. 4, and the learning-rate cross-check in Fig. 5b).

The proposed fixes (Multi-level Noise-perturbed Guidance and width-aware LR scaling) are simple, lightweight, and clearly explained, with an ablation showing MNG outperforms the MSG-GAN baseline and both linear and no-guidance variants.

Strong headline result: GAT-XL/2 reaches FID 2.96 on ImageNet-256 in 40 epochs, competitive with or better than much more heavily trained diffusion/flow and other one-step GAN baselines, while retaining GAN advantages (single-step inference, semantic latent interpolation).

Reasonably thorough scaling study across four model sizes (S–XL) and two patch sizes, plus a GFLOPs-vs-FID correlation analysis (Fig. 3), supporting the central scalability claim within the tested range.

Good supplementary material: detailed hyperparameters/config tables, compute cost reporting, extensive qualitative visualizations (interpolations, per-class samples, feature/attention maps), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a single dataset/resolution (ImageNet-256); no evidence is provided that the approach transfers to other domains, resolutions, or text-conditional settings, limiting the generality of the scalability claim.

The tested model range (29M–602M generator params) is modest relative to the scales at which diffusion/AR models have demonstrated their scaling laws; claims of 'scalability' would be more convincing with at least one larger jump or an explicit scaling-law fit (e.g., loss/FID vs. compute power-law), which is not attempted.

The headline efficiency comparison (40 epochs vs. hundreds/thousands for baselines) is based on epoch counts alone; no wall-clock or FLOPs-normalized training cost comparison to competing methods is given, despite compute cost per iteration differing substantially across GAN/diffusion/AR paradigms.

Table 1's comparison mixes methods with different tricks (ImageNet-pretrained discriminators, CFG, latent-space guidance, REPA) with only brief footnotes to caveat these differences; the extent to which the reported SOTA number depends on the added latent-space guidance versus the core GAT architecture is not fully disentangled (GAT-XL/2 without guidance scores 3.02 vs. 2.96 with, a relatively small gap, but the guidance mechanism itself is borrowed from prior work).

Core technical ingredients (MNG derived from MSG-GAN's multi-scale supervision; the LR scaling rule closely related to Karras et al.'s equalized learning rate) are incremental adaptations rather than fundamentally new mechanisms, somewhat tempering originality.

Ablation studies are performed mostly at small/base scale (GAT-S/2, GAT-B/2); it is not verified whether the same design choices (noise schedule, MNG stage count K=4, alignment weight) remain optimal or necessary at the largest scale (XL), where the main result is reported.
Evaluation relies solely on FID; no precision/recall, diversity, or human evaluation metrics are reported, leaving open questions about mode coverage and sample diversity trade-offs typical of GANs.

The paper lacks any explicit limitations or societal/ethical impact discussion (e.g., misuse potential of realistic generative models, dataset bias in ImageNet), which is a gap in an otherwise carefully written manuscript.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored question -- whether GANs, unlike diffusion/AR models, can be scaled reliably with plain transformer backbones and simple recipes -- and frames it clearly with a concrete diagnosis (early-layer underutilization, scale-coupled optimization instability).

The proposed fixes (Multi-level Noise-perturbed Guidance and a width-aware learning-rate scaling rule) are simple, cheap to implement, and each is supported by a targeted ablation (Fig. 4, Fig. 5a-b) showing the intended mechanism (activation of early layers via LPIPS block-ablation and PCA feature visualization; stable convergence with the adapted LR vs. divergence/slow convergence when swapping configurations).

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation: FID-vs-iteration curves across four model sizes (S–XL) and two patch sizes, a GFLOPs-vs-FID correlation analysis, decoupled G/D scaling study, and a CKNNA representation-alignment analysis, giving a more complete picture than a single headline number.

Competitive quantitative results (FID 2.96 on ImageNet-256, 1-NFE) obtained in substantially fewer training epochs than other GAN baselines (BigGAN, GigaGAN, StyleGAN-XL), together with a reasonably detailed appendix (model configs, hyperparameters, noise schedule derivation, compute budget) that aids reproducibility despite no stated code release.

GANs' distinctive properties (single-step sampling, smooth latent interpolation) are preserved and qualitatively demonstrated (Figs. 11-12), which is a meaningful practical advantage over multi-step diffusion/flow competitors even at comparable FID.
weaknesses: The core contribution is largely a combination of existing techniques (R3GAN's relativistic/gradient-penalty objective, REPA-style representation alignment, MSG-GAN-inspired multi-scale supervision, StyleGAN's equalized-LR idea, ViT/DiT-style modulation) rather than a fundamentally new architectural or theoretical insight; the paper itself frames most pieces as adaptations of prior work, which somewhat limits originality.

The headline SOTA number (FID 2.96) uses an additional latent-space guidance trick (GAT-XL/2*) not clearly matched in all competing baselines, and within the same table a diffusion baseline with REPA (SiT-XL/2+REPA, FID 1.42) substantially outperforms GAT-XL/2, so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is narrowly scoped to 1-NFE GAN methods trained from scratch and could be stated more precisely.

All experiments are conducted on a single dataset/resolution (class-conditional ImageNet-256); no evidence is given for text-to-image, higher resolution, or unconditional settings, which weakens the generality of the 'scalability' claims despite the paper's broad framing in the introduction.

The largest model tested (GAT-XL, ~602M generator parameters) is modest relative to today's billion-parameter-scale generative models; the scaling trend is only shown across a narrow 4-point range (S/B/L/XL), so claims about GAN scalability being 'unlocked' at truly large scale remain speculative.

No repeated runs, variance/error bars, or seed-robustness analysis are reported, which is a notable omission given GAN training is well known to be unstable and sensitive to seed/configuration -- a single FID trajectory per configuration is weak evidence of the claimed 'reliable' training across scales.

Evaluation relies almost exclusively on FID; no precision/recall, diversity metrics, or human evaluation are reported to corroborate perceptual quality and mode coverage claims, and the counter-intuitive CKNNA result (fake features aligning more with the VFM than real features) is noted but not adequately investigated or explained.

The learning-rate scaling rule (Eq. 4) is a heuristic argument based on expected squared norm growing linearly with channel count, without rigorous derivation or comparison to established width-scaling frameworks (e.g., maximal update parametrization/muP), leaving its principled generality and applicability to other axes (depth, batch size) unclear.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem—scalability of GANs—at a time when scaling laws are well studied for diffusion, flow, and autoregressive models but not for adversarial training; this fills a clear gap in the literature.

The proposed GAT framework combines VAE-latent training with a pure ViT-based generator/discriminator, and the paper carefully diagnoses two concrete failure modes (inactive early generator layers, scale-coupled optimization instability) rather than simply proposing an architecture and hoping it works.

The two proposed fixes are simple, lightweight, and well-motivated: Multi-level Noise-perturbed image Guidance (MNG) is a sensible noise-based generalization of MSG-GAN that avoids the resize-induced cross-scale over-constraint the authors identify empirically (Fig. 5a), and the width-aware learning-rate scaling rule (Eq. 4) is derived from a clear, testable argument about update-magnitude invariance.

Empirical validation is fairly thorough: FID-vs-iteration curves across four model sizes (S–XL) and two patch sizes, a strong GFLOPs–FID correlation (-0.95), decoupled G/D scaling analysis, and quantitative block-level LPIPS/PCA analyses that directly substantiate the 'inactive early layers' claim rather than relying on qualitative impressions alone.

Reported results are strong: GAT-XL/2 reaches FID 2.96 (SOTA among 1-NFE generative models on ImageNet-256) in only 40 epochs, 6x fewer than comparable baselines, and the paper reports both the guided (2.96) and unguided (3.02) numbers, allowing readers to gauge the contribution of latent-space guidance.

Good reproducibility support: detailed appendix with full architectural/hyperparameter tables, noise-schedule derivation, per-scale learning rates, and compute-resource disclosure (8xA6000, 12 days), plus extensive qualitative material (interpolations, PCA feature maps, per-class samples).
weaknesses: The ablation studies (MNG, adaptive LR, REPA) are all performed only at the smallest scale (GAT-S/B); it is not verified whether these components remain necessary or have the same relative effect at the L/XL scales where the headline result is obtained, which slightly undercuts the 'scalability' framing.

The headline SOTA number (FID 2.96) depends on an additional test-time 'latent-space guidance' trick (style-space extrapolation, Zhang et al. 2024) applied to 30% of blocks; while the unguided number (3.02) is also reported and still competitive, the main comparison table foregrounds the guided result, and other baselines in the table are trained with very different budgets/epochs/CFG settings, making the SOTA claim comparison somewhat heterogeneous.

All experiments are conducted on a single dataset/resolution (ImageNet-256, class-conditional). No evidence is given for higher resolutions, text-to-image conditioning, or other data domains, so the generality of the proposed scaling recipe beyond this one setting is untested.

The framework layers together many components borrowed from prior work (R3GAN relativistic+gradient-penalty loss, RoPE, SwiGLU-FFN, qk-norm, REPA-style VFM alignment, differentiable augmentation, projection discriminator, MSG-GAN-inspired multi-level supervision); the core novelty is largely in the combination and adaptation rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and with so many simultaneous ingredients it is hard to know how essential each is at scale.

No wall-clock or FLOPs-based training-cost comparison against baselines is given; the 'epoch efficiency' claim doesn't account for the extra per-iteration overhead introduced by MNG's multi-level outputs and the frozen DINOv2 teacher forward pass used for REPA alignment.

Evaluation relies solely on FID; no Precision/Recall, Inception Score, or other diversity/mode-coverage metrics are reported, so classic GAN failure modes (mode collapse, diversity loss) are not quantitatively ruled out beyond qualitative interpolation figures.

The scaling-law claim rests on only four discrete model sizes (S, B, L, XL); while the trend is monotonic, this is a small number of points and no extrapolation/held-out model size test is performed to confirm the rule generalizes beyond the tested range.

strengths: Strong empirical results: GAT-XL/2 achieves FID 2.18 for 1-step class-conditional ImageNet-256 generation with only 60 epochs, a substantial improvement in both quality and training efficiency over prior 1-NFE GANs and diffusion/flow models.

Thorough, well-designed scaling study across model size (S/B/L/XL), patch size, and compute (both inference and cumulative training GFLOPs), showing consistent, near-monotonic improvements and a plausible power-law relationship between compute and FID.

Clear identification of a concrete failure mode (early-layer inactivity in transformer generators) supported by multiple convergent diagnostics: PCA feature visualization, block-ablation LPIPS analysis, and cosine-similarity measurements of block input/output and z-sensitivity.

The proposed Multi-level Noise-perturbed Guidance (MNG) is simple, lightweight, and empirically validated with informative ablations (vs. MSG-GAN-style resizing, linear vs exponential noise schedules), showing consistent gains.

Width-aware learning-rate scaling rule is intuitively motivated, has an accompanying (if simplified) theoretical derivation in the appendix, and is empirically validated via cross-scale learning-rate swap experiments showing it is necessary for stable training across model sizes.

Extensive supplementary experiments strengthen generality claims: higher-resolution (512×512) generation, text-to-image on MS-COCO, unconditional FFHQ generation, robustness to different VAE tokenizers, additional metrics beyond Inception-FID (CLIP-FID, precision/recall), decoupled G/D scaling analysis, compatibility with large-batch training, and latent-space manipulation (interpolation, GANSpace, StyleCLIP) demonstrating retained GAN-specific properties.
Reasonably transparent reporting of implementation details, hyperparameters, and even a seed-robustness check, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The scaling-law fit (FID(C) ≈ 3.52×10^5·C^-0.456) is derived from only 4–5 summary points (one per model size), which is a fairly sparse basis for a power-law claim compared to typical scaling-law studies; the range of scales studied (29M–602M parameters) is also fairly narrow.

The discriminator uses features aligned to a pretrained DINOv2 model (REPA), which raises a similar concern to the one the authors themselves flag for StyleGAN-XL's ImageNet-pretrained discriminator (footnote in Table 1) — i.e., that FID gains may partly reflect alignment with pretrained feature spaces rather than pure image quality. This tension is not clearly addressed, and the ablation showing REPA's large FID improvement (Fig. 5c) makes this concern more salient.

Most core scaling experiments (Fig. 3, ablations) are run for only 20 epochs (50K iterations), a short training regime; it is unclear whether the observed scaling trends, MNG benefits, or LR-rule benefits persist, saturate, or reverse under substantially longer training more comparable to some baselines.

Baseline comparisons in Table 1 span a wide range of training budgets/epochs and architectures, making the FID comparisons not fully controlled; while epoch-efficiency claims are highlighted, compute/wall-clock comparisons (partially addressed in the appendix) are not systematically included in the main text.

No explicit "Limitations" section in the main paper; some potential limitations (e.g., reliance on pretrained VFM/tokenizer, relatively small scale range, single-seed reporting for most results) are only partially discussed in the appendix.

The theoretical justification for the width-aware LR rule (Appendix A.10) relies on a highly simplified single-linear-layer argument and standardized-channel assumptions; while empirically validated, it is not a rigorous derivation for the full transformer architecture with normalization, attention, and residual connections.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored question—whether GANs can be scaled like diffusion/AR transformers—with a clean, minimal-deviation design (pure ViT generator/discriminator in VAE latent space).

Strong empirical headline result: FID 2.18 for 1-NFE ImageNet-256 class-conditional generation, beating prior 1-NFE GAN and diffusion/flow baselines while using substantially fewer training epochs (60 vs. 240-480+).

Thorough and well-designed ablations: MNG variants (MSG/linear/exponential vs. no guidance), adaptive LR cross-check (swapping learning rates between model sizes), REPA ablation, and decoupled generator/discriminator scaling all clearly isolate the contribution of each proposed component.

Good diagnostic methodology for the early-layer inactivity claim: PCA feature visualization, per-block LPIPS ablation, and cosine-similarity analyses (input/output and cross-noise) converge on a consistent story.

Extensive supplementary validation beyond the main table: ImageNet-512 results, MS-COCO text-to-image, FFHQ unconditional generation, alternative VAE tokenizer, CLIP-FID/precision-recall metrics, large-batch compatibility, and seed-robustness checks, which substantially strengthen confidence in the core findings.

Retains characteristic GAN advantages (single-step sampling, smooth latent interpolation, compatibility with GANSpace/StyleCLIP-style editing), which is a meaningful practical selling point over diffusion/AR alternatives.
weaknesses: The 'scaling law' claim (power-law fit in Fig. 3d/24) is derived from only 4 discrete model sizes (S/B/L/XL) with one summary point each; this is a much narrower evidentiary base than typical scaling-law studies and should be described more cautiously (fitted trend vs. established law).

The width-aware learning-rate rule is justified via a single-linear-layer, SGD-style argument (Appendix A.10), but training actually uses AdamW, whose per-parameter gradient normalization already partially decouples update magnitude from activation norm; the theoretical link between the derivation and the observed empirical benefit is not fully rigorous.

Potential fairness/consistency concern in the main comparison table: the paper explicitly flags StyleGAN-XL's FID advantage as partly attributable to an ImageNet-pretrained discriminator, yet GAT's own discriminator is trained with a VFM (DINOv2) alignment loss, which could analogously bias Inception-FID; the CLIP-FID check partially but not fully addresses this asymmetry.

Models are trained for comparatively few epochs (20-60) relative to most baselines, and while framed as 'data efficiency,' it leaves open whether GAT's scaling advantage would persist, saturate, or invert at longer training horizons comparable to baselines' full schedules.

The maximum scale studied (GAT-XL, ~600M generator parameters) is modest relative to the 'scalable/large-scale' framing invoked by the title and motivation; the paper does not demonstrate behavior at the billion-parameter regime where scaling claims are typically most consequential.

Limited statistical robustness reporting: only a small-scale, short-schedule seed-variance check (GAT-S/2, 10 epochs) is provided; no repeated runs or variance estimates for the headline XL result or for the ablation curves.

Some training details (e.g., the mid-training change in gradient-penalty coefficient at epoch 40) suggest schedule-level tuning that is not fully reconciled with the paper's narrative of a single fixed configuration scaling cleanly across model sizes.

strengths: Addresses a clearly underexplored problem—systematic scalability of GANs—by combining VAE-latent training with a pure transformer G/D design, contrasting with prior large-scale GAN efforts (StyleGAN-XL, GigaGAN, TransGAN) that involved heavy task-specific tuning of a single model rather than studying scaling trends.

Diagnoses concrete failure modes with convincing, multi-pronged evidence: PCA feature visualization, per-block LPIPS ablation, and cosine-similarity analyses (input/output and cross-noise sensitivity) all consistently show early-layer inactivity without MNG and its mitigation with MNG.

The two proposed fixes (Multi-level Noise-perturbed Guidance and a width-aware learning-rate rule) are simple, lightweight, and well-motivated, with a (heuristic but reasonable) derivation for the LR scaling rule and clean ablations (Fig. 5a/5b) that isolate their individual contributions.

Strong headline result: GAT-XL/2 reaches FID 2.18 on ImageNet-256 1-NFE generation in only 60 epochs, beating strong one-step baselines (GigaGAN, MeanFlow, Shortcut) with far fewer epochs, and the paper substantiates data efficiency claims with an epoch-to-FID plot.

Extensive, well-executed supplementary analyses that go beyond the core claim: decoupled G/D scaling, CKNNA representation-alignment study, patch-size and tokenizer robustness, high-resolution (512×512) transfer, additional metrics (CLIP-FID, precision/recall) to guard against Inception-FID artifacts, large-batch compatibility, seed-robustness check, and a fitted compute-FID power law—together these substantially strengthen the scalability claim.

Retains and demonstrates GAN-specific advantages (single-step sampling, smooth latent interpolation, compatibility with GANSpace/StyleCLIP editing), reinforcing the practical motivation for reviving GAN research.
Reproducibility is unusually thorough: detailed architecture/hyperparameter tables, noise-schedule formulas, optimizer settings, and per-model learning rates are all reported in the appendix.

Honest limitations discussion (e.g., per-iteration training cost, hardware caveats, discriminator feature erosion during fine-tuning, batch/depth-scaling not yet unified with the width rule) rather than hidden or omitted.
weaknesses: The core techniques (multi-scale/noise-based intermediate supervision reminiscent of MSG-GAN and progressive growing, muP-style width-dependent LR scaling, VFM-based representation alignment borrowed from diffusion REPA) are individually adaptations of existing ideas; the novelty is primarily in the combination and application to transformer GANs rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.

The wall-clock training-time comparison against DiT/MeanFlow (Appendix A.6) is confounded by different GPU hardware (8×A100 vs 8×RTX A6000), making the '18 days vs 36 days' claim only suggestive rather than a controlled comparison; per-iteration cost is acknowledged to be ~5× higher than diffusion.

Model scale remains modest (up to ~600M/468M parameters for G/D) relative to the scaling regimes explored in autoregressive/diffusion scaling-law literature the paper positions itself against; the largest model is only trained to 60 epochs, leaving open whether the favorable trends continue at substantially larger scale or longer schedules without new instabilities.

The width-aware LR derivation (Sec. 2.4, App. A.10) is based on a simplified single-linear-layer toy analysis under idealized unit-variance/normalization assumptions; its extension to depth and batch size is explicitly left as future work (App. A.11), so the 'principled scaling rule' claim is only partially rigorous for the full attention/FFN stack.

The REPA/VFM-alignment component, while ablated, raises a subtlety: since it aligns the discriminator's real-image features to a pretrained DINOv2 model, some of the reported gains could partly reflect leveraging external pretrained representation knowledge rather than purely improved adversarial-scaling mechanics; the CLIP-FID results partially but not fully address the general concern about metric/feature entanglement.

Text-to-image (MS-COCO) and unconditional (FFHQ) extensions are explicitly framed as lightweight, under-tuned first passes with single-run results and no ablations, so their evidentiary weight for generality is limited.

Multi-seed robustness is checked only for the smallest model (GAT-S/2) at a short 10-epoch schedule, leaving uncertainty about run-to-run variance for larger models or the full training length where headline FID numbers are reported.
